title: Perfect is His way
hookLine: perfect is His way and perfect His Word (Sukhmani 24)

cards: The car won't start. The rain comes in sideways. The email you were waiting for says no.

By ten in the morning, the day is clearly not going to be a perfect one. Then Sukhmani's last ashtpadi says something that sounds almost cheeky on a day like that: perfect is His way, and perfect His Word.
It isn't saying the car will start. It's saying something about what lies underneath the day that won't.

teach.h: THE PERFECT GURU, THE PERFECT WORD.
teach.b: The twenty-fourth ashtpadi keeps ringing pooraa, perfect, through its stanzas.
Its first stanza begins, in paraphrase: listen to the teaching of the perfect Guru; see the Supreme as near you; remember God with every breath, and the anxiety of the mind will lift.

teach.h: NOT A CLAIM THAT DAYS FEEL PERFECT.
teach.b: Perfect Guru, perfect Word, perfect way. Here's what perfect is not claiming. It isn't claiming every day will feel perfect, or that bad things don't happen.
Sikh history has martyrdoms in it, Gurus among them. The tradition doesn't pretend life is smooth.
What it claims is something underneath the surface: that God's hukam, God's order, is whole, even when we only see a ragged piece of it.
Sikhs speak of meeting the day that way as bhaanaa mannanaa: accepting bhaanaa, God's will. Guru Arjan, who wrote Sukhmani, sings in another hymn, in paraphrase: whatever You do seems sweet to me.
Sikh tradition remembers that he lived those words to the end. That's the trust this stanza points to. Not pretending the rain isn't sideways; trusting there's a whole beneath the part.
And notice the practical line in the middle: remember God with every breath, and the anxiety lifts.
Saas saas. The trust isn't one big leap. It's breath by breath, on the imperfect day itself.
Perfect underneath, imperfect on top: Sukhmani asks the reciter to live in both.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's last ashtpadi hear of the perfect Guru, Word and way, and meet hard days with bhaanaa, acceptance of God's will, remembering God with each breath.

o: God's will, the order under every day
the feeling of peace after prayer

games.q: perfect is His way — tap the pairs.

s: Sukhmani promises every day will feel perfect
it says God's way is whole underneath, even on imperfect days.
the stanza says remembering God with every breath lifts the mind's anxiety
saas saas: trust practiced breath by breath.
Sikh tradition pretends life is smooth
its history includes martyrdoms, Gurus among them.

games.q: it's ten in the morning and everything's gone wrong. what does the twenty-fourth ashtpadi point toward?
o: decide God's way must be broken.
name the trouble, and trust a whole underneath, breath by breath.
games.why: perfect underneath, imperfect on top. the stanza's practical line: remember God with every breath, and the anxiety of the mind lifts.

practice: Name to yourself, plainly, what's gone wrong today or this week, without arguing with it.

Then, on each breath in, hold the thought, this is the surface, and on each breath out, there's a whole underneath; you don't have to feel the trust, just practice it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath.

wordCard.voice: Bhaanaa, God's will: Sukhmani says God's order and Word are whole even when our day isn't; Sikhs meet it with bhaanaa, breath by breath.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhaanaa, God's will, and the Sikh ideal of accepting it.

carryVoice: Your line: perfect, underneath. Breath by breath, even on the sideways-rain days. That's day five hundred thirty-one.
